editorial.titleTr: 부산에서 세계로: 글로벌 문화유산 협력의 새 장
summaryTr: 유네스코 제48차 세계유산위원회 회의가 부산에서 폐막하며 글로벌 문화유산 협력의 새로운 시대를 열었다.
이번 회의는 세계 각지의 문화유산과 자연유산 보존을 위한 국제적 공약을 더욱 강화했다.
부산의 개최는 인류의 가장 소중한 유산을 미래세대에 위해 보호하려는 노력에 새로운 탄력을 불어넣었다.
editorial.bodyTr:
부산에서 열린 제48차 유네스코 세계유산위원회 회의의 성공적인 마무리는 단순히 11일간의 국제 행사 종료 이상의 의미를 갖는다.

이번 회의는 대한민국이 세계 문화유산 보존과 관리에 있어 국제적 리더십을 발휘할 수 있음을 입증하는 기회가 되었다. 위원회의 결정들은 전 세계의 문화유산 보호 정책에 영향을 미치며, 이는 우리나라의 문화 외교력을 한 단계 높였다는 평가를 받고 있다.

특히 이번 회의에서 논의된 기후변화와 문화유산 보존의 관계에 대한 내용은 앞으로의 국제 논의에 중요한 기초를 마련했다. 우리는 선진국으로서 개발도상국들의 문화유산 보존 사업에 필요한 지원과 경험 공유를 제공할 책임이 있다.

부산에서의 이 성공이 단순한 일회성 행사에 그치지 않기 위해, 정부와 민간이 함께 우리의 문화유산 보존 체계를 더욱 강화하고 발전시켜야 한다. 이는 미래 세대를 위한 우리의 책임이자 세계 무대에서 한국의 위상을 지키는 길이 될 것이다.

editorial.titleTr: Will Markets Keep Tumbling While Leverage Players Duck Responsibility?
summaryTr: Policy Director Kim Yong-beom argues that leveraged ETFs are not the cause of stock market volatility
Leveraged ETFs including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix contribute to expanded volatility
Call for financial authorities to recognize responsibility and promptly devise countermeasures
editorial.bodyTr: Contrary to Deputy Minister Kim Yong-beom's assertion that leveraged ETFs are not a major cause of volatility in the domestic stock market, criticism has been raised that high-risk products such as leveraged ETFs for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have contributed to amplifying volatility. The financial authorities are being called upon to recognize their responsibility and devise swift countermeasures.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Democratic Party Must Bear Full Responsibility for Abolishing Supplementary Investigation Authority
summaryTr: The Democratic Party pushed through legislation to abolish the prosecution's supplementary investigation authority.
Concerns over human rights violations are growing due to the police's monopoly on investigative powers.
Political circles are increasingly bearing responsibility for potential judicial chaos ahead.
editorial.bodyTr: The Democratic Party of Korea has pushed through a revision to the Criminal Procedure Act that strips the prosecution of its supplementary investigative authority, signaling a fundamental shift in the criminal justice system. As concerns grow over potential human rights violations and damage to judicial justice due to police monopolizing investigative powers, the revision faces criticism for being grounded in specific political intentions, with responsibility for any future judicial chaos increasingly being directed at the political establishment.

summaryTr: The government raised the National Pension Fund's stock investment cap for political reasons.
It lost its role as a market circuit breaker during the market crash.
There is a need to establish accountability for unprincipled fund management.
editorials.bodyTr: The National Pension Service lost its role as a market stabilizer during market crashes after raising its stock holdings cap for political reasons. The government's artificial market support policies have ultimately disrupted the management of retirement funds for citizens, and there are urgent calls for accountability regarding principle-free fund operations and measures to prevent future problems.

editorial.titleTr: Editorial: More Dismissals Loom—Who Can Claim Presidential Trial Is Unrelated?
summaryTr: The Democratic Party has submitted a bill to amend the Criminal Procedure Act that would add grounds for dismissal of prosecution to the National Assembly.
The opposition points out that this is 'tailored legislation' designed to resolve the president's judicial risks.
There are concerns about a structure in which a Supreme Court justice appointed by the president could decide to dismiss prosecution in cases involving the president.
editorial.bodyTr: The Democratic Party submitted a bill to amend the Criminal Procedure Act to the National Assembly plenary session on the 30th. In addition to abolishing prosecutors' supplementary investigative authority, the bill adds grounds for courts to dismiss indictments. It is problematic enough that the Democratic Party is pushing ahead with abolishing supplementary investigative authority despite concerns that socially disadvantaged groups will suffer harm. But equally troubling is the amendment to Article 327 of the Criminal Procedure Act on dismissal of indictments, which was quietly inserted into the legislation. The Democratic Party claims it merely codifies Supreme Court precedent, but the opposition and legal community point out this appears to be "tailor-made legislation" designed to legitimately shield President Lee Jae-myung from judicial risk. This criticism is not without reason. The ruling party has attempted to introduce a special prosecutor and cancel indictments, claiming the cases involving the president resulted from prosecutorial misconduct. However, it faced public backlash, as evidenced by the party's defeat in the Seoul mayoral election and other local elections. This time, the Democratic Party added two grounds for dismissing indictments: when indictments are brought following "serious illegal investigations" and when indictments are brought in "flagrant deviation of prosecutorial discretion." Current law specifies only six procedural defects for dismissal, such as when indictment procedures violate the law and are therefore void. The inclusion of subjective terms like "serious" and "flagrant" is difficult to defend against criticism that it opens the door for courts to make politically motivated decisions in political cases. Moreover, while cancellation of indictments is only possible before a first trial verdict, dismissal of indictments can occur at the appellate and supreme court levels through judicial rulings, meaning all cases involving the president could be subject to this. The Democratic Party has already passed a bill to increase the number of Supreme Court justices. Chief Justice Jo Hui-dae's term ends next June. President Lee plans to appoint 22 Supreme Court justices, including a new chief justice, during his tenure. This amounts to filling the composition of the Supreme Court that will make final judgments in cases involving him. If the conditions for dismissing indictments are expanded on top of this, it becomes theoretically possible for justices appointed by President Lee to make dismissal rulings in cases involving President Lee. Being perceived as using changes in law and institutions as a shield for those in power would be a disgrace for the president as well. If, as the Democratic Party claims, this legislation is not intended for any particular individual, the party should stop rushing it through. Yet neither the president nor anyone at the Blue House has said anything. If the amended bill passes through the National Assembly, the president should exercise his veto power to independently uphold judicial independence and alleviate public distrust. That is the path to securing the legitimacy of state governance.

editorial.title: Demographic threshold
editorial.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population. editorials.title: Demographic threshold
editorials.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population.
